Build the radio.
Then turn sound into numbers.

This page picks up where the FM & PM Lab stopped. First we build the machines that make FM and read it back, and the radio that tunes to one station. Then we chop a wave into samples, round them to steps, and send them as bits. Every picture plays by itself. You only need to watch.

message / the real signal what the machine makes error, noise, trouble recovered / correct
Part 1 · Lect 13–14 · Lathi §4.9

Making FM

Two ways to build an FM transmitter. Let the message tune an oscillator directly, or make a tiny, very clean FM and then blow it up. Almost every number in this part is bookkeeping of two values: the carrier and the deviation.

1

Direct FM: let the message tune the oscillator

Think of a playground swing. A short rope swings fast and a long rope swings slowly. An LC circuit is an electrical swing. Its "rope length" is \(\sqrt{LC}\), so it swings at

LC oscillator
\[\omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\]
Smaller C → faster swing → higher frequency.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(L,\ C\)Inductance and capacitance of the oscillator tank.Given in H and F. Watch prefixes: μH = \(10^{-6}\), pF = \(10^{-12}\).

Now replace the capacitor with a varactor, a diode whose capacitance changes with the voltage across it. Feed it the message. When the message goes up, C goes down a little, and the frequency goes up a little. The frequency now follows the message. That is FM, made directly. The circuit is called a VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator).

Why is it linear? Write \(C=C_0-k\,m(t)\). Then

Varactor FM (Lect 13)
\[\omega_i=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L(C_0-km)}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC_0}}\Big(1-\frac{km}{C_0}\Big)^{-1/2}\approx\omega_c\Big[1+\frac{k\,m(t)}{2C_0}\Big]\] \[\omega_i=\omega_c+k_f\,m(t),\qquad k_f=\frac{\omega_c\,k}{2C_0}\]
Valid only while \(km\ll C_0\). Uses \((1-x)^{-1/2}\approx1+x/2\).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(\omega_i\)Instantaneous frequency in rad/s: how fast the angle is growing right now.Differentiate θ(t) with respect to t. Then put in the time asked for.
\(C_0,\ k\)Varactor rest capacitance and its change per volt.Given: "\(C=C_0-km(t)\)" → \(C_0\) is the constant, k the coefficient of m.
\(m(t)\)The message: the information signal (voice, a tone, a pulse train) before modulation.Given as a formula or a graph. In a modulated signal it is the part that is NOT the carrier: in \(A\cos[\omega_ct+k_f\int m]\) it is what sits inside the integral.
\(\omega_c\)Carrier frequency in rad/s (\(=2\pi f_c\)).The coefficient of t in the carrier’s angle: \(\cos(2000\pi t)\) → \(\omega_c=2000\pi\) rad/s.
\(k_f\)FM sensitivity: how many rad/s the frequency moves per volt of message.Given ("\(k_f=2\pi\times10^4\) rad/s/V"), or read it off \(\cos[\omega_ct+k_f\int m]\). Given in Hz/V (e.g. "20 kHz/V")? Then \(\Delta f=k_fm_p\) with no 2π.

Good

Big deviation is easy. Simple circuit.

Bad

An LC carrier drifts with temperature and supply, so it needs automatic frequency control (AFC). Linear only for small \(km/C_0\).

Modern version

A software radio uses an NCO (numerically controlled oscillator). Each clock tick it adds \(k_f\,m[n]\) to a running phase total. That is exactly "phase = running total of frequency", done in a computer (Lect 13 slide 15).

2

The frequency multiplier: squaring doubles the angle

Remember the spinning hand from the FM lab. A wave is \(\cos\theta(t)\). Now push it through a device that squares it:

Square law
\[\cos^2\theta=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cos 2\theta\]
The whole angle doubles. So \(f_c\to2f_c\) and \(\Delta f\to2\Delta f\). β doubles too.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(\theta(t)\)Total angle of the cosine at time t (radians): everything inside cos[ ].Copy everything inside the cosine. \(10\cos(2\pi10^6t+5\sin2000\pi t)\) → \(\theta=2\pi10^6t+5\sin2000\pi t\).
\(f_c\)Carrier frequency in Hz (\(\omega_c=2\pi f_c\) in rad/s).The frequency of the big cosine: \(\cos(2\pi\cdot10^6t)\) → 1 MHz. \(\cos(10^6t)\) → \(\omega_c=10^6\) rad/s, \(f_c=10^6/2\pi\) = 159.2 kHz. Or "a 100 MHz station".
\(\Delta f\)Peak frequency deviation: how far (Hz) the frequency swings away from \(f_c\).FM: \(k_fm_p/2\pi\). PM: \(k_p\dot m_p/2\pi\). Or straight from the text: "deviation 75 kHz", "f swings 99.9–100.1 MHz" → 100 kHz. From an angle \(\beta\sin2\pi f_mt\): \(\Delta f=\beta f_m\).
\(\beta\)Modulation index of FM/PM: deviation measured in "message widths" (no units).\(\beta=\Delta f/B\). For a tone it is the number in front of the sine in the angle: \(\cos(\omega_ct+5\sin\omega_mt)\) → β = 5.

Write \(\theta=\omega_ct+\psi(t)\). Then \(2\theta=2\omega_ct+2\psi(t)\). Everything inside the angle gets multiplied: the carrier and the wiggle. A tripler does the same with \(\cos3\theta\) (from \(\cos^3\)).

Any nonlinear device \(y=a_1x+a_2x^2+a_3x^3+\dots\) makes copies at \(f_c,2f_c,3f_c,\dots\), each with its deviation multiplied by the same number. A bandpass filter picks the copy you want. So a frequency multiplier = nonlinear device + BPF.

Bonus fact (Lect 15 slide 19)

This is why FM survives a cheap nonlinear amplifier. Distortion only makes copies at \(2f_c,3f_c,\dots\), and a BPF at \(f_c\) removes them. In AM the \(a_3x^3\) term puts a \(\tfrac34a_3m^3\) term right inside the band. That distortion can't be filtered out. So FM can use efficient class-C amplifiers.

3

The mixer moves the carrier and never touches Δf

A mixer multiplies the signal by a local oscillator (LO) wave:

Mixer = multiplier + filter
\[\cos(\omega_ct+\psi)\cdot\cos\omega_{LO}t=\tfrac12\cos\big[(\omega_c-\omega_{LO})t+\psi\big]+\tfrac12\cos\big[(\omega_c+\omega_{LO})t+\psi\big]\]
The filter keeps one of the two. The wiggle \(\psi(t)\) comes through untouched.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(\omega_c\)Carrier frequency in rad/s (\(=2\pi f_c\)).The coefficient of t in the carrier’s angle: \(\cos(2000\pi t)\) → \(\omega_c=2000\pi\) rad/s.
\(f_{LO}\)Local-oscillator frequency fed to the mixer.Usually what you solve for. In a superhet: \(f_c\pm f_{IF}\). Check it is inside any stated LO range.
\(\psi(t)\)The wiggle in the angle that carries the message.Everything in the angle except \(\omega_ct\).
Baby version

A multiplier is a zoom lens: it stretches the whole picture, carrier and wiggle together. A mixer is a slide: it slides the picture along the frequency axis but doesn't stretch it. So only multipliers change Δf.

Memory hook · the two-number backpack

The signal carries a backpack with two numbers: (carrier, Δf). A ×n box multiplies both. A mixer changes only the first. A filter changes neither. Every Armstrong question is just carrying this backpack through the boxes.

4

Armstrong: make a tiny clean FM, then blow it up

Direct FM drifts. Armstrong's trick: start with a rock-steady crystal oscillator, make narrowband FM from it, then multiply.

From the FM lab, NBFM is a carrier plus a 90°-shifted DSB term. Each part is easy to build:

NBFM in hardware
\[\varphi_{NBFM}\approx A\cos\omega_ct-A\,k_f\,a(t)\sin\omega_ct,\qquad a(t)=\!\int\! m\,dt\]
Crystal oscillator \(\cos\omega_ct\) · 90° phase shifter → \(\sin\omega_ct\) · integrator → \(a(t)\) · one DSB-SC modulator · an adder.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(A\)Carrier amplitude: the peak height of the carrier wave (volts).The number in front of the carrier cosine. \(10\cos(2\pi10^6t+\dots)\) → A = 10. If only power is given: \(A=\sqrt{2P}\) (200 W → A = 20).
\(\omega_c\)Carrier frequency in rad/s (\(=2\pi f_c\)).The coefficient of t in the carrier’s angle: \(\cos(2000\pi t)\) → \(\omega_c=2000\pi\) rad/s.
\(k_f\)FM sensitivity: how many rad/s the frequency moves per volt of message.Given ("\(k_f=2\pi\times10^4\) rad/s/V"), or read it off \(\cos[\omega_ct+k_f\int m]\). Given in Hz/V (e.g. "20 kHz/V")? Then \(\Delta f=k_fm_p\) with no 2π.
\(a(t)\)Running integral of the message: \(\int m\,dt\).Integrate the message. For \(m=a\cos\omega_mt\): \(a(t)=\frac{a}{\omega_m}\sin\omega_mt\).

The catch: to stay narrowband, the deviation must be tiny, around 10 to 25 Hz. Broadcast FM needs 75 kHz. That is a gain of about 3000.

If you just multiplied by 3000, a 200 kHz carrier would land at 600 MHz. Way too high. So: multiply part of the way, slide the carrier back down with a mixer (Δf unchanged), then multiply the rest of the way.

5

The Armstrong recipe for every exam variant

Name the stages: NBFM at \(f_1\) with deviation \(\Delta f_1\) → ×\(n_1\) → mixer with \(f_{LO}\) → BPF at \(f_{mix}\) → ×\(n_2\) → output \(f_c\), \(\Delta f\).

Three equations, always
\[\textbf{(1) deviation: }\ n_1n_2=\frac{\Delta f}{\Delta f_1}\] \[\textbf{(2) carrier after stage 2: }\ f_c=n_2\,f_{mix}\ \Rightarrow\ f_{mix}=\frac{f_c}{n_2}\] \[\textbf{(3) mixer: }\ f_{mix}=|n_1f_1\pm f_{LO}|\]
Deviation fixes the product. The carrier fixes the split. The mixer fixes the LO.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(n_1\)Frequency multiplication of stage 1 (before the mixer).Unknown you solve for. Must be a whole number; often a product of ×2 and ×3 blocks.
\(n_2\)Frequency multiplication of stage 2 (after the mixer).\(n_2=f_c/f_{mix}\) when the BPF/mixer output frequency is given; else from \(n_1n_2\) and the LO range.
\(\Delta f\)Deviation wanted at the output (the broadcast value).Given: "required deviation 75 kHz".
\(\Delta f_1\)Deviation of the small NBFM signal at the very start.Given ("NBFM at 200 kHz with Δf = 25 Hz"), or \(\beta_1f_m\) with the lowest message frequency (keep β₁ under the stated limit, e.g. 0.25 or 0.5).
\(f_c\)Carrier frequency in Hz (\(\omega_c=2\pi f_c\) in rad/s).The frequency of the big cosine: \(\cos(2\pi\cdot10^6t)\) → 1 MHz. \(\cos(10^6t)\) → \(\omega_c=10^6\) rad/s, \(f_c=10^6/2\pi\) = 159.2 kHz. Or "a 100 MHz station".
\(f_{mix}\)Carrier frequency just after the mixer.\(f_c/n_2\); or given as "the BPF after the mixer is at X".
\(f_1\)Carrier frequency of the NBFM oscillator (stage-1 input).Given: "crystal oscillator at 200 kHz".
\(f_{LO}\)Local-oscillator frequency fed to the mixer.Usually what you solve for. In a superhet: \(f_c\pm f_{IF}\). Check it is inside any stated LO range.
Say it like a story (this is the whole lesson)

You start with a tiny, clean FM: a carrier \(f_1\) and a very small wiggle \(\Delta f_1\). You need a big FM: carrier \(f_c\) and wiggle \(\Delta f\).

  • The wiggle decides HOW MUCH you multiply. Only multipliers grow the wiggle, so all the growth \(\Delta f/\Delta f_1\) must come from \(n_1\times n_2\).
  • The carrier decides WHERE you split. The last box is ×\(n_2\), and it must land exactly on \(f_c\). So whatever leaves the mixer is \(f_c\div n_2\).
  • The mixer fills the GAP. The LO is just the distance between what arrives at the mixer (\(n_1f_1\)) and what must leave it (\(f_c/n_2\)).

Which case am I in? Look at what the question did not give you. That tells you where to start.

What's missingYour first stepTiny example

\(75/8=9.375\) kHz
Traps
  • The mixer never changes Δf. If your answer changes Δf at the mixer, stop.
  • Both \(f_{LO}=n_1f_1-f_{mix}\) and \(n_1f_1+f_{mix}\) work on paper. The allowed LO range decides.
  • "Below 0.25" means strictly less. A pair that needs β exactly 0.25 fails.
Part 2 · Lect 14–15 · Lathi §4.7

Reading FM back

An envelope detector reads height. FM keeps its height fixed. So the trick is always the same: first turn frequency changes into height changes, then read the height.

6

Differentiate: FM turns into AM

Take the FM wave and differentiate it. The chain rule pulls the speed of the angle out in front:

The discriminator idea
\[\varphi_{FM}=A\cos\Big[\omega_ct+k_f\!\int m\Big]\] \[\frac{d\varphi_{FM}}{dt}=-A\big[\omega_c+k_f\,m(t)\big]\sin\Big[\omega_ct+k_f\!\int m\Big]\]
The height is now \(A[\omega_c+k_fm(t)]\). The message is in the height. That's AM.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(A\)Carrier amplitude: the peak height of the carrier wave (volts).The number in front of the carrier cosine. \(10\cos(2\pi10^6t+\dots)\) → A = 10. If only power is given: \(A=\sqrt{2P}\) (200 W → A = 20).
\(\omega_c\)Carrier frequency in rad/s (\(=2\pi f_c\)).The coefficient of t in the carrier’s angle: \(\cos(2000\pi t)\) → \(\omega_c=2000\pi\) rad/s.
\(k_f\)FM sensitivity: how many rad/s the frequency moves per volt of message.Given ("\(k_f=2\pi\times10^4\) rad/s/V"), or read it off \(\cos[\omega_ct+k_f\int m]\). Given in Hz/V (e.g. "20 kHz/V")? Then \(\Delta f=k_fm_p\) with no 2π.
\(m(t)\)The message: the information signal (voice, a tone, a pulse train) before modulation.Given as a formula or a graph. In a modulated signal it is the part that is NOT the carrier: in \(A\cos[\omega_ct+k_f\int m]\) it is what sits inside the integral.

Fast wiggles have steep slopes. So after differentiating, the crowded parts come out tall and the spread-out parts come out short. An envelope detector then traces the tops: \(A[\omega_c+k_fm]\). Block the DC \(A\omega_c\) and you are left with \(A\,k_f\,m(t)\).

The height never goes negative because \(k_fm_p=\Delta\omega\lt\omega_c\) (the deviation is tiny compared with the carrier). So the envelope detector works without distortion.

Exam lens
  • Envelope detector on FM directly: the output is just the constant A. No message (Lect 14 KC1 → B; Lathi 4.7-3 b).
  • Square-wave FM through d/dt: two frequencies become two heights; the envelope is a shifted square wave (Lathi 4.7-2).
7

Put a limiter first

On the way, fading and noise make the height wobble: \(A(t)\cos\theta\). Differentiating that gives an extra \(\dot A\) term, and the envelope now carries \(A(t)\) as well as the message. Bad.

Fix: a bandpass limiter. Clip the wave hard to a fixed level (this keeps every zero crossing, so the frequency survives), then a BPF at \(f_c\) turns the clipped square-ish wave back into a clean sinusoid of constant height.

8

Other ways to turn frequency into height

You don't need a perfect differentiator. Any filter whose \(|H(f)|\) rises in a straight line across \(f_c\pm\Delta f\) does the same job.

  • Slope detector: a tuned LC circuit, with \(f_c\) placed on the rising side of its bell. As \(f_i\) swings, the output height swings with it. (An RC high-pass also works: \(|H|\approx2\pi fRC\) when \(2\pi fRC\ll1\).)
  • Balanced discriminator: two tuned circuits, one above \(f_c\) and one below, outputs subtracted. The S-shaped difference is straight over a wider range, and even-order distortion cancels. The ratio detector is the same idea with built-in amplitude immunity.
  • Zero-crossing detector: a sinusoid at \(f_i\) crosses zero \(2f_i\) times a second. Count the crossings in a short window: the count follows m(t).
  • PLL (phase-locked loop): a VCO chases the incoming wave. To keep it locked, the control voltage must follow the incoming frequency, so that voltage is the message. No inductors, so it fits on a chip (Lect 14 KC2 → B).
9

FM demodulator vs PM demodulator

Write the angle as \(\omega_ct+\psi(t)\). An FM demodulator outputs the speed of the extra angle, \(\dot\psi\). A PM demodulator outputs the extra angle itself, \(\psi\). So, just like the swap rule in the FM lab:

BuildWhat comes outWorks when
FM demod → ∫\(\int\dot\psi=\psi\) → a PM demodulatorm has no jumps, and the DC offset is removed before the integrator. Otherwise a constant offset \(c\) integrates to a ramp \(ct\) that grows forever.
PM demod → d/dt\(\frac{d}{dt}\psi\) → an FM demodulatorAlways. A constant offset differentiates to zero, and the FM phase \(k_f\!\int m\) is continuous even if m jumps.
Baby version

Integrating is like adding up your pocket money every day. If someone slips in one extra rupee every day by mistake (a DC offset), your total drifts away forever. Differentiating looks only at changes, so a fixed mistake vanishes.

10

Why FM sounds better

Put a weak interfering tone \(I\cos(\omega_c+\omega_I)t\) next to the carrier A (with \(I\ll A\)). What leaks out of each detector? (Lect 15 slide 20)

DetectorOutput caused by the interfererRead it as
AM (envelope)\(I\cos\omega_It\)Full strength. A bigger carrier doesn't help.
PM\(\dfrac IA\sin\omega_It\)Shrunk by the carrier, flat with frequency.
FM\(\dfrac{I\,\omega_I}{A}\cos\omega_It\)Shrunk by the carrier, but grows with \(\omega_I\) (FM is the slope of the phase).

Capture effect. Look at it with arrows. The carrier is a long arrow; the interferer is a short arrow spinning on its tip. The phase of the sum only wobbles a little, so the receiver locks onto the stronger station. If the interferer becomes the longer arrow, the receiver suddenly switches to it.

Takeaways
  • FM suppresses a weaker co-channel station: the capture effect. About 6 dB of signal-to-interference is enough, versus about 35 dB for AM.
  • FM noise grows with frequency (∝ ωI). That is the reason for pre-emphasis and de-emphasis.
  • Constant envelope → efficient class-C amplifiers. Nonlinearity only adds harmonics at \(n\omega_c\), removed by a BPF.
Part 3 · Lect 15–16 · superhet deck · Lathi §4.8

The superheterodyne receiver

One great filter that never moves, and a mixer that slides whichever station you want into it. The price is a mirror-image station on the other side of the LO.

11

Bring every station to one fixed place

Picking one station out of its neighbours 10 kHz away needs a very sharp filter. Making a very sharp filter that you can also tune across the whole band is hard.

The superhet's idea: build one sharp, high-gain filter at a fixed frequency, the intermediate frequency (IF). Then, whatever station you want, use a mixer to slide it to the IF. Turning the dial only moves the LO.

antenna→RF amp + broad tunable filter→mixer ← tunable LO→IF amp + sharp fixed filter→detector→audio
Tuning rule
\[f_{IF}=|f_{LO}-f_c|\qquad\text{high-side: } f_{LO}=f_c+f_{IF}\qquad\text{low-side: } f_{LO}=f_c-f_{IF}\]
Standard IFs: 455 kHz (AM radio), 10.7 MHz (FM radio), 38 MHz (analog TV).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(f_{IF}\)Intermediate frequency: the fixed frequency every station is moved to.Given ("IF = 455 kHz", "10.7 MHz"). Defaults if missing: AM radio 455 kHz, FM radio 10.7 MHz.
\(f_{LO}\)Local-oscillator frequency fed to the mixer.Usually what you solve for. In a superhet: \(f_c\pm f_{IF}\). Check it is inside any stated LO range.
\(f_c\)Carrier frequency in Hz (\(\omega_c=2\pi f_c\) in rad/s).The frequency of the big cosine: \(\cos(2\pi\cdot10^6t)\) → 1 MHz. \(\cos(10^6t)\) → \(\omega_c=10^6\) rad/s, \(f_c=10^6/2\pi\) = 159.2 kHz. Or "a 100 MHz station".
12

The image: the evil twin in the mirror

The mixer only cares about the distance from the LO. Any signal 455 kHz from the LO comes out at 455 kHz, whichever side it is on. So the LO is a mirror. The wanted station is on one side. Its mirror image, the same distance on the other side, also gets in.

Image frequency
\[f_{img}=2f_{LO}-f_c\] \[\text{high-side: } f_{img}=f_c+2f_{IF}\qquad\text{low-side: } f_{img}=f_c-2f_{IF}\]
The image is always \(2f_{IF}\) from the wanted station, on the far side of the LO.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(f_{img}\)Image frequency: the other station that also lands on the IF.Asked for. Station → LO is one IF; go one more IF the same way.
\(f_{LO}\)Local-oscillator frequency fed to the mixer.Usually what you solve for. In a superhet: \(f_c\pm f_{IF}\). Check it is inside any stated LO range.
\(f_c\)Carrier frequency in Hz (\(\omega_c=2\pi f_c\) in rad/s).The frequency of the big cosine: \(\cos(2\pi\cdot10^6t)\) → 1 MHz. \(\cos(10^6t)\) → \(\omega_c=10^6\) rad/s, \(f_c=10^6/2\pi\) = 159.2 kHz. Or "a 100 MHz station".
\(f_{IF}\)Intermediate frequency: the fixed frequency every station is moved to.Given ("IF = 455 kHz", "10.7 MHz"). Defaults if missing: AM radio 455 kHz, FM radio 10.7 MHz.
Memory hook

"Station — IF — LO — IF — image." Walk from the station to the LO (one IF), then keep walking the same way for one more IF. You're at the image.

Who stops the image?

Only the RF filter in front of the mixer. Once the image has been mixed down it sits exactly at the IF, on top of your station, and nothing can separate them. So the RF filter's one job is to kill things \(2f_{IF}\) away.

13

High-side vs low-side, LO range, and keeping images out of the band

Why radios use high-side. For the AM band 540–1600 kHz with a 455 kHz IF:

LO rangeLO max / min
High-side \(f_c+455\)995–2055 kHz2.06 (easy to tune)
Low-side \(f_c-455\)85–1145 kHz13.47 (very hard to tune)

The capacitor in the LO's tuning circuit sets the ratio. A 2:1 frequency range needs a 4:1 capacitance swing. 13:1 would need about 180:1. Impossible.

Choosing the IF is a trade-off:

High IFLow IF
Image (2fIF away)far → easy to reject ✔close → hard to reject ✘
IF filter selectivityharder to make sharp → poorer neighbour rejection ✘sharp, high-gain filters are easy ✔
No image inside the band [f₁, f₂] (high-side)
\[f_1+2f_{IF}\ \ge\ f_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_{IF}\ \ge\ \frac{f_2-f_1}{2}\]
The lowest station has the lowest image. If even that one clears the top of the band, they all do.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(f_1,\ f_2\)Lowest and highest station of the tuning band.Given: "AM band 540–1600 kHz" → \(f_1=540\), \(f_2=1600\) kHz.
\(f_{IF}\)Intermediate frequency: the fixed frequency every station is moved to.Given ("IF = 455 kHz", "10.7 MHz"). Defaults if missing: AM radio 455 kHz, FM radio 10.7 MHz.
Double conversion

Two mixers in a row (e.g. 21.4 MHz then 455 kHz). Apply the same rules stage by stage. Each stage has its own LO and its own image, worked out from that stage's input. A high first IF pushes the image far away; a low second IF gives sharp selectivity. You get both.

14

The mirror flips the spectrum: what passes the IF filter?

With a high-side LO the IF is \(f_{IF}=f_{LO}-f_{RF}\). A higher RF line lands at a lower IF. So the spectrum comes out mirror-flipped: the upper sideband sits below the carrier at IF.

A tone AM station is three lines: carrier, and \(\mu/2\) at \(f_c\pm f_m\). Map each line with \(f_{LO}-f\), then ask: is it inside the IF filter? Each surviving line keeps half its amplitude (the mixer's ½).

Part 4 · Lect 17–19 · Lathi 5e §5.1 (4e §6.1)

Sampling

Keep only snapshots of a wave and you can still get the whole wave back, as long as you take them often enough. Most questions are: find the highest frequency, double it, and watch what filters and products do on the way.

15

Snapshots: the sampling theorem

A flip-book is a set of snapshots. Flip fast enough and you see smooth motion. A wave is the same. The question is how many snapshots per second you need.

The fastest wiggle in the signal is at B Hz. To catch every wiggle you need at least two snapshots per wiggle: one near the top, one near the bottom.

Sampling theorem
\[f_s\ \ge\ 2B\qquad\text{Nyquist rate}=2B\ \text{samples/s}\qquad\text{Nyquist interval}=\frac{1}{2B}\ \text{s}\]
B = the highest frequency of a lowpass signal (\(G(f)=0\) for \(|f|>B\)).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
\(B\)Message bandwidth: the HIGHEST frequency in the message (Hz).Tones at 100 Hz and 250 Hz → B = 250 Hz (never the lowest, never the difference). "Speech band-limited to 4 kHz" → B = 4 kHz. Read Hz from \(\cos(2\pi\cdot250t)\) → 250; from \(\cos(500t)\) → 500/2π = 79.6 Hz.
Edge case (Lect 17 CC1)

A pure tone exactly at B, sampled at exactly 2B, can land on its zeros every time: \(\sin(2\pi Bt)\) at \(t=n/2B\) is \(\sin(n\pi)=0\). You rebuild silence. For a pure tone at the band edge you need \(f_s>2B\) strictly.

Real systems sample faster than 2B

Real filters can't cut off like a cliff. Sampling above 2B leaves a gap (a guard band) for the filter's slope. Telephone speech: 3.4 kHz → 8 kHz. CD audio: 20 kHz → 44.1 kHz.

16

What sampling does to the spectrum: photocopies

Ideal sampling = multiplying by a train of impulses, one every \(T_s\). The impulse train is periodic, so it is a sum of tones at \(0,\pm f_s,\pm2f_s,\dots\), each of height \(1/T_s\). Multiplying by each tone shifts the spectrum there. So:

Spectrum of the sampled signal
\[\bar g(t)=g(t)\,\delta_{T_s}(t)=\sum_n g(nT_s)\,\delta(t-nT_s)\] \[\bar G(f)=\frac{1}{T_s}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}G(f-nf_s)\]
Copies of G every \(f_s\), each \(f_s\) times taller. Recover with an ideal LPF of bandwidth B and gain \(T_s\).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(T_s\)Sampling interval: time between two samples (\(1/f_s\)).\(1/f_s\). 8 kHz → 125 μs.
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
\(G(f)\)Spectrum (Fourier transform) of the message g(t).From the transform table. Its last non-zero frequency is B.
\(g(nT_s)\)The n-th sample value.Put \(t=nT_s\) into g(t).
Baby version

Sampling is a photocopier that prints your spectrum again and again along the frequency axis, \(f_s\) apart. The LPF is scissors that cut out the middle copy. Scissors only work if the copies don't overlap.

17

Bandwidth algebra: the Nyquist rate of a combined signal

The exam rarely hands you B. It hands you a recipe: add these, multiply those, square that, filter it. You need to know what each step does to the highest frequency.

Operation (bandwidths B₁, B₂)Bandwidth of the resultWhy
\(g_1+g_2\)\(\max(B_1,B_2)\)spectra add, nothing new appears
\(g_1g_2\)\(B_1+B_2\)spectra convolve, widths add
\(g^2\), \(g^m\)\(2B\), \(mB\)repeated convolution
\(g\cos2\pi f_0t\) (seen as lowpass)\(f_0+B\)shifted out to \(\pm f_0\)
\(\dot g\), \(\int g\), \(g(t-t_0)\), \(t\,g(t)\), \((1+at)g\)\(B\) (unchanged)×\(j2\pi f\), ÷\(j2\pi f\), a phase, \(dG/df\): all zero where G is zero
\(g(at)\)\(|a|B\)squeezing in time spreads in frequency
through an LPF of cutoff \(f_L\)\(\min(B,f_L)\)the filter removes the rest
\(\mathrm{sinc}(Wt)\) / \(\mathrm{sinc}^2(Wt)\) (Lathi's sinc)\(\frac{W}{2\pi}\) / \(\frac{W}{\pi}\)rect / triangle spectrum
\(\Pi(t/\tau)\), \(\delta(t)\), any time-limited pulse∞ (needs a filter)sinc / flat spectrum
The method, every time
  1. Break products of sinusoids into single sinusoids (\(\cos^2x=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cos2x\), \(\sin a\cos b=\tfrac12[\sin(a+b)+\sin(a-b)]\)). List every frequency.
  2. Apply any filter: keep only what passes.
  3. B = the largest surviving frequency. Nyquist rate = 2B.
  4. For sinc or pulse signals, use the width rules in the table.
Lathi's notation (it changes the numbers)

Lathi writes \(\mathrm{sinc}(x)=\frac{\sin x}{x}\) (not normalised). \(\Pi(x)=1\) for \(|x|\lt\frac12\). \(\Delta(x)\) is a triangle of total width 1. So \(\mathrm{sinc}(Wt)\) has bandwidth \(W/2\pi\) Hz, \(\Pi(t/\tau)\leftrightarrow\tau\,\mathrm{sinc}(\pi f\tau)\), \(\Delta(t/\tau)\leftrightarrow\frac\tau2\mathrm{sinc}^2(\pi f\tau/2)\). Exam papers sometimes use the normalised \(\sin(\pi x)/\pi x\) instead (2025 Compre Q2). Check which one.

18

Aliasing: the wagon wheel

In old films a fast-spinning wheel looks like it turns slowly, or even backwards. The camera samples too slowly, so a fast motion poses as a slow one. That is aliasing.

In the spectrum: if \(f_s\lt2B\), the copy at \(f_s\) reaches below \(f_s/2\) and lands on the baseband copy. Two damages: the part of G above \(f_s/2\) is lost, and it comes back folded about \(f_s/2\).

Where a tone ends up
\[f_{alias}=|f_0-k f_s|\quad\text{with k chosen so the result is in }[0,\ f_s/2]\]
Lect 17 CC2: 100, 350, 550 Hz at \(f_s=500\) → 100, 150, 50 Hz.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(f_0\)Frequency of the tone being sampled.From the signal: \(\cos(2\pi\cdot350t)\) → 350 Hz.
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
\(k\)A whole number (0, 1, 2, …) picked to bring the alias into 0 … \(f_s/2\).Try k = round(\(f_0/f_s\)).
Antialiasing filter

Once folded, nothing can separate true from fake content. So put an analog LPF with cutoff \(f_s/2\) before the sampler. You lose the tail above \(f_s/2\), but nothing folds back. Lathi 5.1-8 shows this halves the error energy.

19

Getting the wave back: sinc pulses, ZOH, FOH, equaliser

The ideal LPF's impulse response is a sinc. So the LPF puts a sinc pulse on every sample and adds them up:

Ideal (sinc) interpolation, \(f_s=2B\)
\[g(t)=\sum_n g(nT_s)\,\mathrm{sinc}\big(2\pi B(t-nT_s)\big)\] \[E=T_s\sum_n g^2(nT_s)\]
Each sinc is 1 at its own sample and 0 at every other sample. The sincs are orthogonal with energy \(T_s\) each, so the energy is just \(T_s\times\) the sum of squared samples.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(g(nT_s)\)The n-th sample value.Put \(t=nT_s\) into g(t).
\(T_s\)Sampling interval: time between two samples (\(1/f_s\)).\(1/f_s\). 8 kHz → 125 μs.
\(B\)Message bandwidth: the HIGHEST frequency in the message (Hz).Tones at 100 Hz and 250 Hz → B = 250 Hz (never the lowest, never the difference). "Speech band-limited to 4 kHz" → B = 4 kHz. Read Hz from \(\cos(2\pi\cdot250t)\) → 250; from \(\cos(500t)\) → 500/2π = 79.6 Hz.

A real pulse \(p(t)\) gives \(\tilde g=\sum g(nT_s)p(t-nT_s)=p*\bar g\), so \(\tilde G(f)=P(f)\cdot\frac1{T_s}\sum G(f-nf_s)\). The pulse's spectrum P(f) bends the baseband copy. Undo it with an equaliser:

Equaliser
\[E(f)\,P(f)=T_s\ \ \text{for }|f|\le B,\qquad E(f)=0\ \ \text{for }|f|\ge f_s-B\]
Between B and \(f_s-B\) (the guard band) E can be anything.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(E(f),\ P(f)\)Equaliser response and the pulse-shape spectrum.P(f) is the transform of the reconstruction pulse (rect for ZOH: \(T_s\,\text{sinc}\)). E is what you design.
\(T_s\)Sampling interval: time between two samples (\(1/f_s\)).\(1/f_s\). 8 kHz → 125 μs.
\(B\)Message bandwidth: the HIGHEST frequency in the message (Hz).Tones at 100 Hz and 250 Hz → B = 250 Hz (never the lowest, never the difference). "Speech band-limited to 4 kHz" → B = 4 kHz. Read Hz from \(\cos(2\pi\cdot250t)\) → 250; from \(\cos(500t)\) → 500/2π = 79.6 Hz.
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
ZOHFOH
pulserect of width \(T_s\) (0 to \(T_s\))triangle of base \(2T_s\)
outputstaircasestraight lines between samples
\(P(f)\)\(T_s\,\mathrm{sinc}(\pi fT_s)e^{-j\pi fT_s}\)\(T_s\,\mathrm{sinc}^2(\pi fT_s)\) (× delay if made causal)
equaliser\(e^{j\pi fT_s}/\mathrm{sinc}(\pi fT_s)\)\(1/\mathrm{sinc}^2(\pi fT_s)\)
hardwaresample-and-hold; ∫, delay \(T_s\), subtractneeds one future sample (non-causal) → delay by \(T_s\)
20

Real samplers: natural, flat-top, averaging

Real switches stay closed for a short time \(T_q\), not an instant.

  • Natural (gated) sampling: multiply g by a train of rectangles of width \(T_q\). The pulse tops follow the curve. The pulse train is \(C_0+\sum2C_n\cos n\omega_st\) with \(C_0=T_q/T_s\) (the duty cycle), so the baseband part is \(\frac{T_q}{T_s}g(t)\), undistorted. An ideal LPF of bandwidth B and gain \(T_s/T_q\) gives g back.
  • Flat-top (sample-and-hold): each pulse is held at the value \(g(nT_s)\). That is \(p*\bar g\), so the spectrum is multiplied by P(f), a sinc. This droop is the aperture effect. Fix it with \(1/P(f)\).
  • Averaging sampler: each sample is \(\int g(t)q(t-nT_s)dt\). That is g passed through a filter, then ideally sampled. Equalise with 1/Q(f). This needs \(Q(f)\ne0\) for \(|f|\le B\).
21

PAM, PWM, PPM, and time-division multiplexing

The sample values can set a pulse's height (PAM), width (PWM, also PDM) or position (PPM). These are still analog, since the values are continuous. PCM goes further: round the value and send bits.

TDM. A sampled signal is empty between samples. So N signals can take turns on one wire. A rotating switch (the commutator) takes one sample, or n bits, from each channel per turn. One turn = one frame, \(T_f=1/f_s\).

TDM rates
\[\text{PAM-TDM pulse rate}=N f_s\qquad\text{PCM-TDM bit rate } R_b=N\,f_s\,n\]
Lect 18 KC1: 4 × 8000 = 32 000 pulses/s. Deck slide 15: 4 × 8 kHz × 8 = 256 kb/s. Mixed inputs: just add the rates.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(N\)Number of signals sharing the line (TDM channels).Count them: "4 voice channels" → N = 4.
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
\(n\)Bits per sample.Given ("8-bit PCM"), or from L: \(n=\log_2L\). Rounded up to a whole number.
\(R_b\)Bit rate (bits per second).\(nf_s\) for one channel; × N channels for TDM. DM: \(R_b=f_s\).
FDM vs TDM

FDM gives each signal its own frequency band all the time (radio, OFDM). It needs guard bands and linear amplifiers. TDM gives each signal all the band for a short slot. It needs synchronisation.

Part 5 · Lect 18–19 · Lathi 5e §5.2

PCM: round it, number it, send the number

After sampling, each sample is still any real number. PCM rounds it to one of \(L=2^n\) shelves and sends the shelf's n-bit number. Every PCM question uses some of four moves: Δ, noise, bits, companding.

22

The PCM chain, and why digital wins

sampler→quantiser→encoder→line + regenerative repeaters→decoder→LPF

The only step you can never undo is the quantiser (the rounding). Everything after it is exact, because a repeater only has to decide "is this a 0 or a 1?" and send out a fresh, clean pulse.

23

The uniform quantiser: a staircase ruler

Split the range \([-m_p,\,m_p]\) into L equal steps. Each step is

Step size
\[\Delta=\frac{2m_p}{L},\qquad L=2^n\]
Your keys use mid-rise levels at the centre of each step: \(-m_p+(k+\tfrac12)\Delta\), \(k=0,\dots,L-1\). Code k in plain binary, so the lowest level is 00…0.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(\Delta\)Step size: height of one quantiser step.\(2m_p/L\). Or from "error at s(0) = 0 is 0.25 V" (mid-rise) → Δ = 0.5 V.
\(m_p\)Peak of the message: the largest value of |m(t)|.Tone \(a\cos\omega_mt\) → \(m_p=a\). Graph → read the highest point (or deepest dip, whichever is bigger in size). Several tones → add their amplitudes (worst case). Asymmetric message → use \((m_{max}-m_{min})/2\).
\(L\)Number of quantisation levels (\(=2^n\)).\(2^n\): 3 bits → 8, 8 bits → 256. From an error spec: \(L\ge m_p/q_{max}\), then up to a power of 2.
\(n\)Bits per sample.Given ("8-bit PCM"), or from L: \(n=\log_2L\). Rounded up to a whole number.
\(k\)Level number (0 = bottom). Its binary is the PCM code.\(k=\text{round}\big(\frac{x+m_p}{\Delta}-\frac12\big)\), clipped to 0 … L−1.
Which level does a sample x go to?
\[k=\operatorname{round}\!\Big(\frac{x+m_p}{\Delta}-\frac12\Big),\ \text{clipped to }0\ldots L-1\]
Error \(q=x-\hat x\). Inside the range, \(|q|\le\Delta/2\).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(k\)Level number (0 = bottom). Its binary is the PCM code.\(k=\text{round}\big(\frac{x+m_p}{\Delta}-\frac12\big)\), clipped to 0 … L−1.
\(x\)One sample value to be quantised.Put the sample time into the message: \(x=m(nT_s)\).
\(m_p\)Peak of the message: the largest value of |m(t)|.Tone \(a\cos\omega_mt\) → \(m_p=a\). Graph → read the highest point (or deepest dip, whichever is bigger in size). Several tones → add their amplitudes (worst case). Asymmetric message → use \((m_{max}-m_{min})/2\).
\(\Delta\)Step size: height of one quantiser step.\(2m_p/L\). Or from "error at s(0) = 0 is 0.25 V" (mid-rise) → Δ = 0.5 V.
\(L\)Number of quantisation levels (\(=2^n\)).\(2^n\): 3 bits → 8, 8 bits → 256. From an error spec: \(L\ge m_p/q_{max}\), then up to a power of 2.
\(q\)Quantisation error: sample minus its level.\(x-\hat x\). Never more than Δ/2 in size inside the range.
Mid-rise, not mid-tread

With mid-rise there is no level at 0. Levels sit at \(\pm\Delta/2,\pm3\Delta/2,\dots\). That's how 2025 Q3 tells you Δ: "s(0) = 0 has error 0.25 V" means the nearest level is ±0.25, so Δ = 0.5 V.

24

Quantisation noise and SQNR: +6 dB per bit

For a busy signal the error is equally likely anywhere in \([-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]\). Its average power is the average of \(q^2\) over that strip:

Build it up in four lines
\[N_q=\overline{q^2}=\frac1\Delta\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2}q^2\,dq=\frac{\Delta^2}{12}\] \[N_q=\frac{(2m_p/L)^2}{12}=\frac{m_p^2}{3L^2}\] \[\text{SQNR}=\frac{\overline{m^2}}{N_q}=3L^2\,\frac{\overline{m^2}}{m_p^2}\] \[\text{SQNR}_{dB}=4.77+6.02\,n+10\log_{10}\frac{\overline{m^2}}{m_p^2}\]
One more bit doubles L, multiplies SQNR by 4, adds 6.02 dB.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(N_q\)Quantisation-noise power.\(\Delta^2/12\) (PCM); \(E^2/3\) (DM).
\(q\)Quantisation error: sample minus its level.\(x-\hat x\). Never more than Δ/2 in size inside the range.
\(\Delta\)Step size: height of one quantiser step.\(2m_p/L\). Or from "error at s(0) = 0 is 0.25 V" (mid-rise) → Δ = 0.5 V.
\(m_p\)Peak of the message: the largest value of |m(t)|.Tone \(a\cos\omega_mt\) → \(m_p=a\). Graph → read the highest point (or deepest dip, whichever is bigger in size). Several tones → add their amplitudes (worst case). Asymmetric message → use \((m_{max}-m_{min})/2\).
\(L\)Number of quantisation levels (\(=2^n\)).\(2^n\): 3 bits → 8, 8 bits → 256. From an error spec: \(L\ge m_p/q_{max}\), then up to a power of 2.
\(\text{SQNR}\)Signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio.\(\overline{m^2}/N_q\); in dB: \(10\log_{10}\) of that.
\(\overline{m^2}\)Message power: the average of m² over time.Tone of peak a → \(a^2/2\). Square wave ±a → \(a^2\). Triangle or sawtooth of peak a → \(a^2/3\). Several tones → add their \(a^2/2\).
\(n\)Bits per sample.Given ("8-bit PCM"), or from L: \(n=\log_2L\). Rounded up to a whole number.
Conditions you must state
  • \(\Delta^2/12\) assumes no clipping (signal inside \([-m_p,m_p]\)) and a busy signal. It fails for very few levels or a near-constant input.
  • 1.76 + 6.02n is only the special case of one full-scale sine (\(\overline{m^2}/m_p^2=\tfrac12\)). For multi-tone signals (2024 Q4, Lect 19 twin) it is wrong. Use the 4.77 form, or compute \(\overline{m^2}/N_q\) directly.
  • Sum of tones: \(m_p\) = sum of amplitudes (worst case, all cosines peak at t = 0). Power = sum of \(A_i^2/2\) (only when the frequencies differ).
Memory hook

"Twelve for a strip, three for a staircase." Uniform error on ±Δ/2 → Δ²/12. Swap Δ = 2m_p/L and the 12 becomes 3L²: SQNR = 3L² × (power ÷ peak²).

25

Bits cost bandwidth

Bit rate and minimum bandwidth
\[R_b=n\,f_s\qquad B_T\ge\frac{R_b}{2}\qquad(\text{at } f_s=2B:\ B_T=nB)\]
The minimum (Nyquist) bandwidth to send \(R_b\) pulses per second is \(R_b/2\).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(R_b\)Bit rate (bits per second).\(nf_s\) for one channel; × N channels for TDM. DM: \(R_b=f_s\).
\(n\)Bits per sample.Given ("8-bit PCM"), or from L: \(n=\log_2L\). Rounded up to a whole number.
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
\(B_T\)Transmission bandwidth: width of the band the modulated signal occupies.Asked for. Carson: \(2(\Delta f+B)\). DSB/AM: 2B. SSB: B. PCM: \(R_b/2\) minimum.
\(B\)Message bandwidth: the HIGHEST frequency in the message (Hz).Tones at 100 Hz and 250 Hz → B = 250 Hz (never the lowest, never the difference). "Speech band-limited to 4 kHz" → B = 4 kHz. Read Hz from \(\cos(2\pi\cdot250t)\) → 250; from \(\cos(500t)\) → 500/2π = 79.6 Hz.

Each extra bit costs one more B of bandwidth and buys 6 dB. So SNR grows exponentially with bandwidth. That trade is PCM's superpower.

The reverse trade (2026 Q5A, Lathi 5.2-8): keep \(R_b\) fixed, sample more slowly (but still above Nyquist), and spend the saved rate on more bits per sample.

Telephone numbers to know

B = 3.4 kHz (often modelled as 4 kHz), \(f_s=8\) kHz, n = 8 → 64 kb/s per voice channel.

Bits from an error spec

"Maximum error ≤ x% of \(m_p\)": max error is \(\Delta/2=m_p/L\). So \(L\ge100/x\). Then round up to a power of 2 (L ≥ 200 → 256, never 128).

26

Companding: the same quality for loud and quiet talkers

With uniform steps, Δ²/12 is fixed. A quiet talker has small \(\overline{m^2}\), so their SQNR is poor. Fix: before quantising, compress, which stretches small values up and squashes big ones. Quiet sounds then use many shelves. At the receiver, expand back. Compress + expand = compand.

μ-law
\[y=\frac{\ln(1+\mu|x|/m_p)}{\ln(1+\mu)}\,\mathrm{sgn}(x)\] \[\text{SQNR}\approx\frac{3L^2}{[\ln(1+\mu)]^2}\qquad\text{valid when }\ \mu^2\,\frac{\overline{m^2}}{m_p^2}\gg1\]
The signal power has dropped out. SQNR no longer depends on how loud you talk. Use ln, not log₁₀.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(\mu\)Companding constant (μ-law, not AM’s μ).Given: "μ = 255" (USA), 100 in textbook problems.
\(x\)One sample value to be quantised.Put the sample time into the message: \(x=m(nT_s)\).
\(m_p\)Peak of the message: the largest value of |m(t)|.Tone \(a\cos\omega_mt\) → \(m_p=a\). Graph → read the highest point (or deepest dip, whichever is bigger in size). Several tones → add their amplitudes (worst case). Asymmetric message → use \((m_{max}-m_{min})/2\).
\(L\)Number of quantisation levels (\(=2^n\)).\(2^n\): 3 bits → 8, 8 bits → 256. From an error spec: \(L\ge m_p/q_{max}\), then up to a power of 2.
\(\text{SQNR}\)Signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio.\(\overline{m^2}/N_q\); in dB: \(10\log_{10}\) of that.
\(\overline{m^2}\)Message power: the average of m² over time.Tone of peak a → \(a^2/2\). Square wave ±a → \(a^2\). Triangle or sawtooth of peak a → \(a^2/3\). Several tones → add their \(a^2/2\).
Quick dB rule for μ-law
\[\text{SQNR}_{dB}\approx\alpha+6.02\,n,\qquad \alpha=10\log_{10}\frac{3}{\ln^2(1+\mu)}\]
α = −8.51 dB for μ = 100, and −10.1 dB for μ = 255.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(\text{SQNR}\)Signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio.\(\overline{m^2}/N_q\); in dB: \(10\log_{10}\) of that.
\(\alpha\)Fixed dB offset of the μ-law rule.\(10\log_{10}[3/\ln^2(1+\mu)]\): −8.51 dB (μ = 100), −10.1 dB (μ = 255).
\(n\)Bits per sample.Given ("8-bit PCM"), or from L: \(n=\log_2L\). Rounded up to a whole number.
\(\mu\)Companding constant (μ-law, not AM’s μ).Given: "μ = 255" (USA), 100 in textbook problems.
Companding is not free

For a signal that is already loud (Lathi 5.2-6, \(\overline{m^2}/m_p^2=0.12\)), μ-law needs one bit more than uniform for the same SQNR. Its value is that the SQNR stays the same for quiet talkers.

Part 6 · Lect 20–22 · Lathi 5e §5.5–5.6

DPCM, ADPCM, DM, ADM: send only the surprise

Neighbouring samples are nearly equal. So guess the next one and send only how wrong the guess was. Delta modulation takes this to the limit: one bit per sample, "up one step" or "down one step".

27

DPCM: predict, subtract, quantise, rebuild

If you tell a friend the temperature every hour, you don't say "27.3°" each time. You say "up 0.2". Those changes are small numbers, so they need fewer shelves for the same precision.

The DPCM loop, one sample at a time
\[\text{guess: }\hat m_q[k]\ \ (\text{e.g. } m_q[k-1])\] \[\text{surprise: }d[k]=m[k]-\hat m_q[k]\quad\to\quad\text{quantise: } d_q[k]=d[k]+q[k]\] \[\text{rebuild: }m_q[k]=\hat m_q[k]+d_q[k]=m[k]+q[k]\]
The rebuilt sample is off by exactly one quantisation error. Errors do not pile up.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(m[k]\)The k-th true sample.From the table of samples in the question, in order.
\(\hat m_q[k]\)The guess (prediction) of the k-th sample.First order: the previous rebuilt value \(m_q[k-1]\). Start value is given (usually 0).
\(d[k]\)The surprise: true sample minus guess.\(m[k]-\hat m_q[k]\).
\(d_q[k]\)The quantised surprise actually sent.Find which quantiser band d falls in; use that band’s output value.
\(m_q[k]\)The rebuilt sample (what the receiver has).Guess + \(d_q\).
\(q\)Quantisation error: sample minus its level.\(x-\hat x\). Never more than Δ/2 in size inside the range.
DPCM gain over PCM (same bits)
\[G_p=\frac{\overline{m^2}}{\overline{d^2}}\approx\Big(\frac{m_p}{d_p}\Big)^2\]
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(G_p\)Prediction gain: how much smaller the surprise is than the signal.\(\overline{m^2}/\overline{d^2}\approx(m_p/d_p)^2\).
\(\overline{m^2}\)Message power: the average of m² over time.Tone of peak a → \(a^2/2\). Square wave ±a → \(a^2\). Triangle or sawtooth of peak a → \(a^2/3\). Several tones → add their \(a^2/2\).
\(m_p\)Peak of the message: the largest value of |m(t)|.Tone \(a\cos\omega_mt\) → \(m_p=a\). Graph → read the highest point (or deepest dip, whichever is bigger in size). Several tones → add their amplitudes (worst case). Asymmetric message → use \((m_{max}-m_{min})/2\).
\(d_p\)Peak size of the surprise d.Tone with previous-sample guess: \(2A_m\sin(\omega_mT_s/2)\).
Why the guess must use m_q, not m

The receiver only has the rebuilt values \(m_q\). If the transmitter guessed from the true m, its guesses would slowly drift away from the receiver's, and the quantisation errors would accumulate. Building the guess from \(m_q\) keeps both ends in step.

28

ADPCM: let the step size breathe

A 2-bit DPCM quantiser has outputs \(\pm0.5\Delta,\pm1.5\Delta\). On a steep climb even \(1.5\Delta\) is too small, so the rebuild lags. ADPCM adapts Δ after every sample: an outer code (11 or 00, "big surprise") grows Δ; an inner code (10 or 01, "small surprise") shrinks it. In Lect 21: ×1.6 after outer, ×0.7 after inner.

29

Delta modulation: one bit, a staircase, two kinds of error

DM is DPCM with a 1-bit quantiser. Each sample, the staircase moves up one step E (bit 1) or down one step (bit 0). The receiver is an accumulator (adds up ±E) followed by an LPF. To make one step enough, DM samples many times faster than Nyquist.

DM
\[m_q[k]=m_q[k-1]\pm E,\qquad R_b=f_s\ \ (\text{one bit per sample})\]
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(m_q[k]\)The rebuilt sample (what the receiver has).Guess + \(d_q\).
\(E\)DM step size: how much the staircase moves each sample (volts).Given ("step 0.1 V"), or the minimum: \(E=\dot m_p/f_s\).
\(R_b\)Bit rate (bits per second).\(nf_s\) for one channel; × N channels for TDM. DM: \(R_b=f_s\).
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
No slope overload
\[E\,f_s\ \ge\ \Big|\frac{dm}{dt}\Big|_{max}\qquad\text{tone: } E\,f_s\ge2\pi f_mA_m\]
The staircase's top speed is E per sample = \(Ef_s\) volts per second. It must beat the message's steepest slope. For a band of tones, use the highest frequency.
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(E\)DM step size: how much the staircase moves each sample (volts).Given ("step 0.1 V"), or the minimum: \(E=\dot m_p/f_s\).
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
\(f_m\)Message (modulating) tone frequency in Hz.From the message cosine: \(\cos(2\pi\cdot5000t)\) → 5 kHz; \(\sin(2000\pi t)\) → 1 kHz.
\(A_m\)Peak amplitude of the message tone.Number in front of the message cosine.
Granular noise
\[|q|\le E\qquad N_q=\frac{E^2}{3}\qquad N_o=\frac{E^2}{3}\cdot\frac{B}{f_s}\]
The error is uniform on ±E (not ±E/2), so its power is \((2E)^2/12=E^2/3\). It is spread flat up to \(f_s\); the receiver's LPF keeps only the fraction \(B/f_s\).
What each letter means · how to get it from a question
\(q\)Quantisation error: sample minus its level.\(x-\hat x\). Never more than Δ/2 in size inside the range.
\(E\)DM step size: how much the staircase moves each sample (volts).Given ("step 0.1 V"), or the minimum: \(E=\dot m_p/f_s\).
\(N_q\)Quantisation-noise power.\(\Delta^2/12\) (PCM); \(E^2/3\) (DM).
\(N_o\)Noise power left after the receiver’s lowpass filter.\(\frac{E^2}{3}\cdot\frac{B}{f_s}\) for DM.
\(B\)Message bandwidth: the HIGHEST frequency in the message (Hz).Tones at 100 Hz and 250 Hz → B = 250 Hz (never the lowest, never the difference). "Speech band-limited to 4 kHz" → B = 4 kHz. Read Hz from \(\cos(2\pi\cdot250t)\) → 250; from \(\cos(500t)\) → 500/2π = 79.6 Hz.
\(f_s\)Sampling rate: samples taken per second.Given, or asked. Nyquist: \(f_s=2B\). From a period: \(f_s=1/T_s\).
Which noise formula?

"Quantisation noise power" with no receiver filter mentioned: \(E^2/3\) (slides). After the LPF, or whenever an SNR is asked (2026 Q5B, Lathi 6.7-1): \(\frac{E^2}{3}\frac{B}{f_s}\). Both assume no slope overload. Say which one you use. And the max granular error is E, not E/2.

30

Adaptive DM, and the four schemes side by side

The bits themselves say what's going on. A run of equal bits (111…) means the staircase is lagging, so grow the step. Alternating bits (1010…) mean it is hunting around a flat signal, so shrink the step.

PCMDPCMDMADM
bits/samplenfewer than PCM11
sampling≈ Nyquist≈ Nyquistheavily oversampledoversampled
noiseΔ²/12Δ²/12 on a smaller rangegranular + slope overloadboth reduced
complexitymediumpredictor loopsimplestsimple + step logic
Part 7

The exam toolkit and every formula to memorise

Almost every question in these chapters is one of eight moves. Find the move, then do it. Below the moves are flash cards: read the question, say the answer out loud, then tap.

MOVE 1

Carry the backpack

(carrier, Δf) through every box. ×n multiplies both. Mixer moves the carrier only.

MOVE 2

Mirror at the LO

\(f_{IF}=|f_{LO}-f|\). Image \(=2f_{LO}-f_c\). High-side flips the spectrum.

MOVE 3

List frequencies, filter, double

Break products into tones, apply filters, B = highest left, \(f_s=2B\).

MOVE 4

Fold the alias

\(|f_0-kf_s|\) into \([0,f_s/2]\).

MOVE 5

Δ, then noise

\(\Delta=2m_p/L\), \(N_q=\Delta^2/12\), SQNR = power / \(N_q\). Use real power, not 1.76.

MOVE 6

Snap and code

Index \(k=\mathrm{round}((x+m_p)/\Delta-\tfrac12)\), level \(-m_p+(k+\tfrac12)\Delta\), code k in binary.

MOVE 7

Count bits

\(R_b=nf_s\), \(B_T=R_b/2\). TDM: add the rates. μ-law: \(3L^2/\ln^2(1+\mu)\).

MOVE 8

Out-climb the slope

DM: \(Ef_s\ge\) steepest slope. Noise \(\frac{E^2}{3}\frac{B}{f_s}\). Staircase: ±E per bit.

2026 Midsem Q3(A)5 marks≈ 9 min

Superhet with a drifting LO: which lines get through the IF filter?

Given
  • High-side LO, nominal 1455 kHz, actually 1458 kHz
  • Ch 1: 1000 kHz, μ = 0.5, fm = 2 kHz
  • Ch 2: 1010 kHz, μ = 0.8, fm = 4 kHz
  • IF filter: 450–460 kHz, ideal
Asked
  • IF ranges of both channels
  • Which lines pass
  • \(v_{IF}(t)\)

Spot it: "superheterodyne", "LO drift", "IF filter passband" → lesson 14. Tone AM = three lines. Map every line with \(f_{IF}=f_{LO}-f\). The order flips.

Hint

Write each AM signal as three lines: carrier (amplitude 1) and two sidebands (amplitude μ/2) at \(f_c\pm f_m\). Then \(f_{IF}=1458-f\) for each.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • \(f_{IF}=455\) kHz, high-side LOso \(f_{LO}=f_c+455\)
  • Channel 1: \([1+0.5\cos2\pi(2000)t]\cos2\pi(1000\text{k})t\)\(\mu_1=0.5\), \(f_{m1}=2\) kHz
  • Channel 2: \([1+0.8\cos2\pi(4000)t]\cos2\pi(1010\text{k})t\)\(\mu_2=0.8\), \(f_{m2}=4\) kHz
  • LO drifted to 1458 kHzinstead of 1455 kHz
  • IF filter passes 450–460 kHzideal
Find

(1) the IF ranges of both channels; (2) which lines pass the filter; (3) \(v_{IF}(t)\).

Understand it fully · what a mixer does to each line

Treat each AM signal as three separate lines: carrier (amplitude 1) and two sidebands (amplitude \(\mu/2\)) at \(f_c\pm f_m\). Expanding \([1+\mu\cos\omega_mt]\cos\omega_ct=\cos\omega_ct+\frac{\mu}{2}\cos(\omega_c-\omega_m)t+\frac{\mu}{2}\cos(\omega_c+\omega_m)t\) shows this.

The mixer multiplies each line by \(\cos\omega_{LO}t\). Using \(\cos a\cos b=\frac12[\cos(a-b)+\cos(a+b)]\), every line of frequency \(f\) moves to \(f_{LO}-f\) (the difference, which the IF filter is near) and to \(f_{LO}+f\) (far away, filtered out). Its amplitude is halved.

Because it's \(f_{LO}-f\), a higher RF line lands lower at IF: the order flips (mirror image). That doesn't matter for AM: it's still a carrier with two sidebands.

The drift moves every IF line up by 3 kHz. That pushes part of the neighbour station into the IF filter.

Part 1 · map every line: IF = 1458 − f
  1. Channel 1 lines: 998 kHz (LSB, amp 0.25), 1000 kHz (carrier, amp 1), 1002 kHz (USB, amp 0.25).
  2. IF: \(1458-998=460\), \(1458-1000=458\), \(1458-1002=456\) kHz.Range \([456,\ 460]\) kHz.
  3. Channel 2 lines: 1006 kHz (LSB, amp 0.4), 1010 kHz (carrier, amp 1), 1014 kHz (USB, amp 0.4).
  4. IF: \(1458-1006=452\), \(1458-1010=448\), \(1458-1014=444\) kHz.Range \([444,\ 452]\) kHz.
Ch 1: 456–460 kHz · Ch 2: 444–452 kHz
Part 2 · which lines pass 450–460 kHz
  1. Ch 1: 456 ✓, 458 ✓, 460 ✓ (on the edge; ideal filter passes it).All three pass.
  2. Ch 2: 452 ✓ (inside!), 448 ✗, 444 ✗.Only its 452 kHz line (from its LSB at 1006 kHz) leaks in.
All of Ch 1 (456, 458, 460 kHz) + Ch 2's 452 kHz line
Part 3 · write v_IF(t)
  1. Mixer halves every amplitude.Ch 1: carrier \(1\to0.5\), sidebands \(0.25\to0.125\).Those three lines form an AM signal at 458 kHz: \(0.5[1+0.5\cos2\pi(2000)t]\cos2\pi(458\text{k})t\).
  2. Ch 2's leaked line: amplitude \(0.4\to0.2\) at 452 kHz: \(0.2\cos2\pi(452\text{k})t\).
\(v_{IF}(t)=0.5\,[1+0.5\cos2\pi(2000)t]\cos2\pi(458\times10^3)t+0.2\cos2\pi(452\times10^3)t\)
Trap: Using 1455 instead of 1458; using \(f-f_{LO}\) (gives negative numbers); forgetting the ½ from the mixer; checking only the carriers (the leak is a sideband).
Final answers
Ch 1 range456–460 kHzCh 2 range444–452 kHzpassesall of Ch 1 + 452 kHzv_IFAM at 458 kHz (0.5) + 0.2 cos at 452 kHz

Armstrong: find n₁, n₂ and fLO

Given
  • NBFM: 100 kHz, Δf₁ = 10 Hz
  • BPF after the mixer at 1.635 MHz
  • LO allowed 10–11 MHz
  • Output 98.1 MHz, 75 kHz
Asked
  • \(n_1\), \(n_2\), \(f_{LO}\)

Spot it: "NBFM", "multiplier", "mixer", "75 kHz" → Armstrong recipe (lesson 5). The BPF frequency is given, so \(n_2\) falls out at once.

Hint

Only \(n_2\) acts after the BPF: \(n_2=98.1/1.635\).

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • NBFM source: \(f_1=100\) kHz, \(\Delta f_1=10\) Hzstart
  • target: \(f_c=98.1\) MHz, \(\Delta f=75\) kHzend
  • BPF after the mixer at 1.635 MHzfixes the carrier between mixer and \(n_2\)
  • LO adjustable 10–11 MHz; multipliers ×2, ×3, ×5stock room
Find

\(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(f_{LO}\).

Understand it fully · what each box does to (carrier, deviation)

Track the pair (carrier, Δf) through each box.

A ×n multiplier turns \(\cos(\omega_ct+\phi)\) into \(\cos(n\omega_ct+n\phi)\): it multiplies both the carrier and Δf by n.

A mixer (multiply by the LO, keep one product) gives \(\cos((\omega_c\pm\omega_{LO})t+\phi)\): it shifts the carrier but leaves φ, and so Δf, untouched.

So only the multipliers can grow Δf: the total multiplication \(n_1n_2\) must take 10 Hz to 75 kHz. The mixer exists only to put the carrier where \(n_2\) needs it.

Step 1 · total multiplication from the deviation
\(n_1n_2=\dfrac{\Delta f_{out}}{\Delta f_1}\)
symbolvalue to put inwhere it comes from
\(\Delta f_{out}\)75 000 Hztarget deviation
\(\Delta f_1\)10 HzNBFM deviation
  1. \(n_1n_2=75\,000/10=7500\).
fx-991CW
75 ×10x 3 ÷ 10 EXE
screen shows 7500
Step 2 · n₂ from the carrier after the BPF

After the BPF the carrier is 1.635 MHz, and only \(n_2\) acts after that, so \(n_2\times1.635=98.1\).

  1. \(n_2=98.1/1.635=60\) (\(=2\times2\times3\times5\): two doublers, a tripler, a quintupler ✓).
fx-991CW
98.1 ÷ 1.635 EXE
screen shows 60
Step 3 · n₁, then the carrier before the mixer
  1. \(n_1=7500/60=125\) (\(=5\times5\times5\), three quintuplers ✓).
  2. Carrier after \(n_1\): \(125\times100\) kHz \(=12.5\) MHz.
fx-991CW
Ans ÷ 60 EXE
screen shows 125
right after the 7500
Step 4 · f_LO

The mixer must move 12.5 MHz to 1.635 MHz: \(|12.5-f_{LO}|=1.635\) or \(12.5+f_{LO}=1.635\) (impossible).

  1. \(f_{LO}=12.5-1.635=10.865\) MHz (inside 10–11 ✓) or \(12.5+1.635=14.135\) MHz (outside the range ✗).
\(n_1=125,\ n_2=60,\ f_{LO}=10.865\) MHz
Trap: Thinking the mixer changes Δf. Choosing 14.135 MHz (valid on paper, but outside the stock oscillator's 10–11 MHz).

Find integer N₁, N₂ from an NBFM source, an LO, and a β limit

Given (104 MHz version)
  • NBFM at 200 kHz; audio 15 kHz; β₁ below 0.25
  • Mixer adds 10 MHz
  • Output 104 MHz, 75 kHz
Asked
  • A valid integer pair N₁, N₂

Spot it: no Δf₁ is given, only a β limit. So the deviation equation gives a minimum product, and the carrier equation decides the integers. This is the "β limit" case in lesson 5.

Hint

(1) \(N_1N_2\ \gt\ \Delta f/(\beta_{max}f_m)\). (2) \(N_2(N_1f_1+f_{LO})=f_c\) (or \(N_2(f_{LO}-N_1f_1)\) when the mixer subtracts). Solve (2) for \(N_1\) and try integer \(N_2\).

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • Five versions of one question (2025 Quiz 2). Worked in full for the 104 MHz version; the table gives the rest.
  • 104 MHz version: NBFM at \(f_1=200\) kHz, audio \(B=15\) kHz, \(\beta_{initial}<0.25\)
  • target \(f_c=104\) MHz, \(\Delta f=75\) kHz; mixer ADDS a 10 MHz LOchain: ×N₁ → mixer → ×N₂
Find

Whole numbers \(N_1\), \(N_2\) that meet every requirement.

Understand it fully · two equations, one integer hunt

Two facts fix everything. (1) Deviation: only the multipliers grow Δf, so \(N_1N_2\times\Delta f_1=75\) kHz. The NBFM deviation is limited by β: \(\Delta f_1=\beta f_m\le\beta_{max}f_m\). That gives a minimum product \(N_1N_2\ge\Delta f/(\beta_{max}f_m)\).

(2) Carrier: follow the carrier through: \(f_1\to N_1f_1\to N_1f_1+f_{LO}\) (mixer adds) \(\to N_2(N_1f_1+f_{LO})\). This must equal the target carrier. That equation has only certain whole-number solutions.

Strategy: list the whole-number pairs from the carrier equation, throw out the ones whose product is too small, and pick the one with the smallest product (fewest stages, least noise multiplication). That's what the key does.

Step 1 · minimum product from the deviation
\(N_1N_2>\dfrac{\Delta f}{\beta_{max}f_m}\)
symbolvalue to put inwhere it comes from
\(\Delta f\)75 kHztarget deviation
\(\beta_{max}\)0.25"below 0.25"
\(f_m\)15 kHzaudio bandwidth
  1. \(\beta_{max}f_m=0.25\times15=3.75\) kHz (largest allowed NBFM deviation).
  2. \(N_1N_2>75/3.75=20\).
Step 2 · carrier equation (work in MHz)
  1. After ×N₁: \(0.2N_1\) MHz.After the mixer (adds 10): \(0.2N_1+10\).After ×N₂: \(N_2(0.2N_1+10)=104\).
  2. Solve for N₁: \(0.2N_1+10=\dfrac{104}{N_2}\) → \(N_1=\dfrac{104/N_2-10}{0.2}=\dfrac{520}{N_2}-50\).
  3. N₁ must be a positive whole number: \(N_2\) must divide 520 and be less than 10.4.So \(N_2\in\{1,2,4,5,8,10\}\).

Step 4 · keep the valid ones, pick the smallest product
  1. Products \(N_1N_2\): 470, 420, 320, 270, 120, 20.
  2. (2, 10) has product 20, which needs β exactly 0.25: not allowed ("below 0.25") ✗.

  4. Check the chain: 200 kHz × 15 = 3 MHz → + 10 = 13 MHz → × 8 = 104 MHz ✓.
104 MHz version: \(N_1=15,\ N_2=8\)
The other four versions (same method)

Write the carrier equation, solve it for N₁ in terms of N₂, use the Table app for N₂ = 1, 2, 3, …, keep whole numbers with a big enough product, pick the smallest product. For a mixer that subtracts (\(f_{LO}-N_1f_1\)) the equation becomes \(N_2(f_{LO}-N_1f_1)=f_c\).

  1. 100.1 MHz (300 kHz, LO 11 MHz subtracts, β ≤ 0.3, 10 kHz): product ≥ 75/3 = 25.\(N_2(11-0.3N_1)=100.1\) → \(N_1=\dfrac{11-100.1/N_2}{0.3}\).Pairs: (11, 13), (33, 91).Answer N₁ = 11, N₂ = 13.
  2. 158.4 MHz (200 kHz, LO 20 MHz adds, β ≤ 0.2, 15 kHz): product ≥ 75/3 = 25.\(N_1=\dfrac{158.4/N_2-20}{0.2}\).Pairs: (692, 1), (296, 2), (164, 3), (98, 4), (32, 6).Answer N₁ = 32, N₂ = 6.
  3. 94.5 MHz (150 kHz, LO 15 MHz adds, β ≤ 0.4, 5 kHz): product ≥ 75/2 = 37.5.\(N_1=\dfrac{94.5/N_2-15}{0.15}\).Pairs: (530, 1), (215, 2), (110, 3), (26, 5), (5, 6) — the last has product 30 < 37.5 ✗.Answer N₁ = 26, N₂ = 5.
  4. 101.5 MHz, 80 kHz (250 kHz, LO 12 MHz subtracts, β < 0.25, 10 kHz): product > 80/2.5 = 32.\(N_1=\dfrac{12-101.5/N_2}{0.25}\).Pairs: (19, 14), (34, 29), (41, 58), … Answer N₁ = 19, N₂ = 14.
Trap: Forgetting the units (keep everything in MHz in the carrier equation); taking the first pair you find instead of checking the product limit; for "below 0.25", a product exactly at the limit is NOT allowed.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator

Understand it fully · work backwards through the ×8

The ×8 multiplier multiplies both the carrier and Δf by 8. So at the BPF (just before it) everything is ⅛ of the output. The mixer only shifts the carrier; it does not change Δf. So the FM modulator itself already has the BPF's Δf.

  2. Deviation there: \(75/8=9.375\) kHz.

Image from an LO; double-conversion images; minimum IF

Spot it: image = the mirror of the station in the LO: \(2f_{LO}-f_c\) (lesson 12). "No image in the band" → \(f_{IF}\ge(f_2-f_1)/2\) (lesson 13).

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • 2024 Quiz 1 Q2: tuned to 617 kHz, LO at 1013 kHz
  • 2025 Quiz 2: 150 MHz signal, IF₁ = 21.4 MHz (high-side), IF₂ = 455 kHz (low-side)double conversion
Find

The image frequencies (and, from the guide, the minimum IF for a 41–92 MHz band with high-side LO).

Understand it fully · the image is the station's mirror about the LO

A mixer produces \(|f-f_{LO}|\). Two different input frequencies give the same IF: the station (IF below the LO for high-side) and the image (IF above the LO). So the image is always on the other side of the LO, one IF away from it: \(f_{img}=2f_{LO}-f_c\).

2024 Q2
  1. \(f_{IF}=1013-617=396\) kHz (LO above → high-side).
  2. Image \(=f_{LO}+f_{IF}=1013+396=1409\) kHz (same as \(f_c+2f_{IF}\)).
1409 kHz

  1. Stage 1 (high-side): \(f_{LO1}=150+21.4=171.4\) MHz → image₁ \(=171.4+21.4=192.8\) MHz.
  2. Stage 2 input is 21.4 MHz; low-side: \(f_{LO2}=21.4-0.455=20.945\) MHz → image₂ \(=20.945-0.455=20.49\) MHz (the mirror below the LO).
192.8 MHz and 20.49 MHz
Minimum IF for a 41–92 MHz band (high-side)
  1. Images lie at \(f_c+2f_{IF}\).The lowest one (from 41 MHz) must be above the band: \(41+2f_{IF}\ge92\).
  2. \(f_{IF}\ge(92-41)/2=25.5\) MHz.

Envelope detector on FM; why PLLs

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • KC1: FM straight into an envelope detector
  • KC2: why PLLs instead of slope detectors
Find

The right option for each.

KC1 → (B)

FM keeps its amplitude A constant; only the angle moves. An envelope detector reads the amplitude, so it outputs a constant DC level ∝ A. No message. (That's why an FM discriminator first differentiates: d/dt turns frequency changes into amplitude changes.)

KC2 → (B)

Slope detectors need tuned LC circuits with bulky inductors and only have a narrow linear region. A PLL is active circuitry: it fits on a chip, tracks the frequency linearly and handles noise better.

Final answers
KC1(B) constant DC ∝ AKC2(B) linearity, noise, no inductors

FM demod + integrator = PM demod; PM demod + d/dt = FM demod

Spot it: FM demod outputs \(\dot\psi\); PM demod outputs \(\psi\) (lesson 9). Then ask what a DC offset and a jump do to each.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • (a) FM demodulator → integrator; (b) PM demodulator → differentiator
Find

Show (a) gives a PM demodulator when m has no jumps, and why the DC offset must be removed first; show (b) works even with jumps or DC offset.

Understand it fully · what each demodulator outputs

Write the received angle as \(\omega_ct+\psi(t)\). A PM demodulator outputs \(\psi\) (the phase). An FM demodulator outputs \(\dot\psi\) (the frequency deviation). Real ones may add a constant offset c.

(a) FM demodulator + integrator, input is PM
  1. PM: \(\psi=k_pm(t)\).FM demodulator gives \(\dot\psi+c=k_p\dot m+c\).
  2. Integrate: \(k_pm(t)+ct\).The ct term is a ramp that grows forever and swamps the output → remove the DC before integrating.
  3. If m jumps, \(\dot m\) has an impulse that a real (band-limited) demodulator can't produce, so the integral misses the step → m must have no jumps.
(b) PM demodulator + differentiator, input is FM
  1. FM: \(\psi=k_f\int m\), which is continuous even if m jumps.
  2. PM demodulator gives \(\psi+c\).Differentiate: \(k_fm(t)\); the constant c disappears.
  3. Works with jumps and with DC offset ✓.
Final answers
(a) works if m has no jumps and DC is removed(b) always works
Lathi 5e 4.7-2= 4e 5.4-2≈ 8 min

Bandwidth; envelope detector alone; differentiate then detect; recover m(t)

Spot it: peel off \(\omega_ct\) to get ψ. Differentiate ψ for Δf (FM lab move 1). Then the discriminator chain.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • \(s=2\cos[10^7\pi t+2\sin(1000\pi t+0.3\pi)-3\pi\cos2000t]\)
  • \(k_f=200\pi\)for part (d)
Find

(a) bandwidth; (b) envelope detector output; (c) output if differentiated first; (d) which can give m, and m(t).

Step 1 · the phase deviation and its derivative
  1. \(\psi=2\sin(1000\pi t+0.3\pi)-3\pi\cos2000t\).
  2. \(\dot\psi=2\times1000\pi\cos(1000\pi t+0.3\pi)+3\pi\times2000\sin2000t=2000\pi\cos(\cdot)+6000\pi\sin2000t\).
(a) bandwidth
  1. Peak: \(\Delta\omega=2000\pi+6000\pi=8000\pi\) → \(\Delta f=4000\) Hz.
  2. Message frequencies: 1000π rad/s = 500 Hz, and 2000 rad/s = 318 Hz → \(B=500\) Hz.
  3. \(B_T=2(4000+500)=9000\) Hz = 9 kHz.
(b) envelope detector directly
  1. Amplitude is constant: output = 2 (DC, no information).
(c) differentiate first
  1. Amplitude becomes \(2[10^7\pi+\dot\psi]\) (always positive since \(10^7\pi\gg8000\pi\)).
  2. Output: \(2\times10^7\pi+4000\pi\cos(1000\pi t+0.3\pi)+12\,000\pi\sin2000t\).
(d) recover m
  1. Use (c): remove the DC, divide by 2 to get \(\dot\psi\), then \(m=\dot\psi/k_f\).
  2. \(m=\dfrac{2000\pi}{200\pi}\cos(\cdot)+\dfrac{6000\pi}{200\pi}\sin2000t=10\cos(1000\pi t+0.3\pi)+30\sin2000t\).
Final answers

Spot it: time-limited inputs have infinite bandwidth, but the filters cut them off. A filter output is bandlimited to the filter edge. Product → bandwidths add (lesson 17).

Hint

The rect's sinc has its first zero at \(\omega=2\pi/\tau=20k\pi\), exactly the edge of \(H_1\). Convert rad/s to Hz before doubling.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • \(g_1=10^4[u(t+\frac{1}{2\times10^4})-u(t-\frac{1}{2\times10^4})]\)a rectangular pulse, height \(10^4\), width \(10^{-4}\) s
  • \(g_2=\delta(t)\)an impulse
  • \(H_1\): passes \(\omega
  • \(H_2\): passes \(\omega
  • \(y=y_1y_2\)multiplied

Understand it fully · a filter output can't be wider than the filter

An ideal low-pass filter with edge \(\omega_0\) cuts off everything above it. Whatever goes in, the output is band-limited to \(\omega_0\) rad/s, i.e. \(B=\omega_0/2\pi\) Hz. Nyquist rate = \(2B\).

Input 1: a rectangle of width τ has a sinc spectrum whose first zero is at \(\omega=2\pi/\tau\). Here \(\tau=10^{-4}\) s, so the first zero is at \(2\pi\times10^4=20k\pi\), exactly the filter edge. The filter keeps the whole main lobe.

Input 2: an impulse contains every frequency equally (\(\delta\leftrightarrow1\)), so the output spectrum is just the filter shape: a flat rectangle up to \(10k\pi\).

Product: multiplying two signals convolves their spectra, so the bandwidths add.

Step 1 · Y₁ and its Nyquist rate
  1. \(G_1(\omega)=10^4\cdot10^{-4}\,\text{sinc}\!\left(\dfrac{\omega\times10^{-4}}{2}\right)=\text{sinc}\!\left(\dfrac{\omega}{2\times10^4}\right)\): height 1, zeros at \(\pm20k\pi\).
  2. \(Y_1=G_1H_1\): the main lobe only, edge \(20k\pi\) rad/s.
  3. \(B_1=\dfrac{20k\pi}{2\pi}=10\,000\) Hz → \(f_{s,1}=2\times10=20\) kHz.

Step 3 · y = y₁y₂

  2. \(f_s=2\times15=30\) kHz.

(a) Nyquist rate after a 250 Hz LPF; (b) PAM, PWM or PPM from the formula

Spot it: (a) products of sinusoids + a filter → the method in lesson 17. (b) Ask which property of p the sample changes: delay, height, or time-scale (lesson 21).

Hint

\(\cos^2\) makes DC and a doubled frequency. \(\sin a\cos b\) makes a sum and a difference frequency. The difference can sneak under the filter.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • (a) \(x(t)=3\cos200\pi t+4\sin300\pi t+2[\cos400\pi t]^2+5\sin600\pi t\cos1000\pi t\)into an LPF with cutoff 250 Hz
  • (b) \(x_1=\sum p(t-nT_s-m(nT_s))\), \(x_2=\sum m(nT_s)p(t-nT_s)\), \(x_3=\sum p\big(\frac{t-nT_s}{m(nT_s)}\big)\)identify the pulse modulation
Find

(a) the Nyquist rate of the filter output; (b) PAM, PWM or PPM for each.

Understand it fully · the recipe for "Nyquist rate after a filter"

1. Break x(t) into single sinusoids (expand squares and products). 2. Write each one's frequency in Hz: \(\cos(2\pi f t)\) means f; so \(\cos(400\pi t)\) is 200 Hz. 3. Keep only those below the filter cutoff. 4. Nyquist rate = 2 × the highest one that survived (not 2 × the cutoff).

(a) Step 1 · turn every term into single tones
  1. \(3\cos200\pi t\): \(200\pi=2\pi\times100\) → 100 Hz.
  2. \(4\sin300\pi t\): 150 Hz.
  3. \(2\cos^2400\pi t=1+\cos800\pi t\) (using \(\cos^2A=\dfrac12+\dfrac12\cos2A\)): DC (0 Hz) and 400 Hz.
  4. \(5\sin600\pi t\cos1000\pi t=\dfrac52[\sin1600\pi t+\sin(-400\pi t)]\) (using \(\sin A\cos B=\dfrac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]\)): 800 Hz and 200 Hz.
(a) Step 2 · filter, then double
  1. All tones: 0, 100, 150, 200, 400, 800 Hz.Cutoff 250 Hz keeps 0, 100, 150, 200 Hz.
  2. Highest surviving: 200 Hz → Nyquist rate \(=2\times200=400\) Hz.
(a) 400 Hz
(b) What does the sample change?
  1. \(x_1\): each pulse is shifted in time by \(m(nT_s)\) → position ∝ m → PPM.
  2. \(x_2\): each pulse is multiplied by \(m(nT_s)\) → height ∝ m → PAM.
  3. \(x_3\): each pulse's time axis is divided by \(m(nT_s)\) → stretched, width ∝ m → PWM.
Trap: Forgetting the 400 Hz and DC inside cos², or the 200 Hz difference from sin·cos (it passes the filter). Answering 500 Hz (2 × the cutoff).
Final answers
(a) Nyquist rate400 Hzx₁PPMx₂PAMx₃PWM

Reconstruct from 9 samples: x(0.005) and the energy

Spot it: "reconstructed from its sample values" + a sinc sum → the interpolation formula, and energy = \(T_s\sum x^2[n]\) (lesson 19). Here sinc is the normalised one, \(\sin\pi x/\pi x\).

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • \(B=50\) Hz, sampled at the Nyquist rate
  • \(x(t)=\sum x(nT_s)\,\text{sinc}(t/T_s-n)\)sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx) here
  • \(x(nT_s)=-1\) for \(-4\le n\le0\); \(+1\) for \(1\le n\le4\); 0 otherwise9 samples
Find

\(x(0.005)\) and the energy of x(t).

Understand it fully · sinc interpolation

Each sample launches its own sinc pulse, centred on its sample time, that is 1 at its own sample and 0 at every other sample. The signal is the sum of all these pulses. To find x at an in-between time, add each sample × its sinc evaluated there.

Energy: the shifted sincs don't overlap in energy (they're orthogonal), and each carries \(T_s\) of energy per unit² of sample. So \(E=T_s\sum x^2[n]\).

Step 1 · where is t = 0.005 between the samples?
  1. Nyquist rate \(=2B=100\) Hz → \(T_s=1/100=0.01\) s.
  2. \(t/T_s=0.005/0.01=0.5\): exactly halfway between n = 0 and n = 1.
Step 2 · add up the sincs at 0.5
  1. \(x(0.005)=\sum_{n=-4}^{4}x[n]\,\text{sinc}(0.5-n)\).
  2. Pair them up: n = 0 (−1) and n = 1 (+1) give \(-\text{sinc}(0.5)+\text{sinc}(-0.5)=0\) (sinc is even).Likewise (−1, 2), (−2, 3), (−3, 4) all cancel.
  3. Left over: n = −4: \(-\text{sinc}(0.5+4)=-\text{sinc}(4.5)\).
  4. \(\text{sinc}(4.5)=\dfrac{\sin4.5\pi}{4.5\pi}=\dfrac{1}{4.5\pi}=0.0707\) (\(\sin4.5\pi=1\)).
  5. \(x(0.005)=-\dfrac{1}{4.5\pi}=-\dfrac{2}{9\pi}=-0.0707\).

  1. \(\sum x^2[n]=9\times1=9\).
  2. \(E=T_s\times9=0.01\times9=0.09\) J.

Understand it fully · copies every f_s

Ideal sampling makes copies of the spectrum at every multiple of \(f_s\) (each scaled by \(f_s\)). Recovery is possible only if the copies don't overlap, i.e. \(f_s\ge2B\).

(a) g₁ at 7.5 kHz
  1. Needs 10 kHz; 7.5 is too slow.

(b) g₂ at 25 kHz
  1. Needs 24 kHz; 25 is enough.
  2. Copies at multiples of 25 kHz leave a 1 kHz gap (12 to 13 kHz) → recoverable with an LPF whose edge falls in that gap.

Equalisers for four reconstruction pulses; sketch the interpolated signals

Spot it: "equalizer filter to recover g" → \(E(f)=T_s/P(f)\) for \(|f|\le B\) (lesson 19). So the whole job is: find P(f) of each pulse.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • four reconstruction pulses: (a) \(\Pi(t/T_s-\frac12)\); (b) \(\Delta(t/T_s-\frac12)\); (c) half-sine on \([0,T_s/2]\); (d) \(\Delta(t/2T_s)\)
Find

The equaliser E(f) for each; sketch the interpolated signals (5.1-6).

Understand it fully · the equaliser undoes the pulse

Reconstructing with a pulse p(t) multiplies the spectrum by P(f). To get g back exactly, the equaliser must cancel it in the message band: \(E(f)=T_s/P(f)\) for \(|f|\le B\) (anything in the guard band, 0 beyond \(f_s-B\)).

The four pulses
  1. (a) rect on \([0,T_s]\): \(P=T_s\,\text{sinc}(\pi fT_s)e^{-j\pi fT_s}\) → \(E=\dfrac{e^{j\pi fT_s}}{\text{sinc}(\pi fT_s)}\).
  2. (b) triangle on \([0,T_s]\): \(P=\dfrac{T_s}{2}\text{sinc}^2(\dfrac{\pi fT_s}{2})e^{-j\pi fT_s}\) → \(E=\dfrac{2e^{j\pi fT_s}}{\text{sinc}^2(\pi fT_s/2)}\).
  3. (c) half-sine on \([0,T_s/2]\): \(P=\dfrac{T_s}{\pi}\dfrac{\cos(\pi fT_s/2)}{1-f^2T_s^2}e^{-j\pi fT_s/2}\) → \(E=\dfrac{\pi(1-f^2T_s^2)}{\cos(\pi fT_s/2)}e^{j\pi fT_s/2}\).
  4. (d) triangle on \([-T_s,T_s]\) (FOH): \(P=T_s\,\text{sinc}^2(\pi fT_s)\) → \(E=1/\text{sinc}^2(\pi fT_s)\).

5.1-6 sketches: (a) staircase, (b) sharp tents back to 0, (c) half-sine bumps, (d) straight lines joining the sample tops. Only (d) looks like g before equalising.

Spot it: Parseval: error energy = \(\int|G-\tilde G|^2df\). Without an AAF the error is the lost tail plus the folded tail. With an AAF only the lost tail (lesson 18).

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • \(G=5\,\Delta(f/800)\)triangle, height 5, reaching ±400 Hz

Understand it fully · two kinds of error

Without an anti-aliasing filter you lose twice: the part of G above 350 Hz is lost, and it also folds back on top of the band (aliasing). With an AAF at 350 Hz the folding is gone; only the lost tail remains. Parseval lets you compute error energy directly in frequency: \(E=\int|G-\tilde G|^2df\).

(a), (b) without AAF
  1. Copies every 700 Hz; neighbours overlap from 300 to 400 Hz.
  2. Folded error for 300 < f < 350: \(5\dfrac{f-300}{400}\).Lost part for 350 < f < 400: \(5\dfrac{400-f}{400}\).Both are ramps over 50 Hz.
  3. One piece: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{50}\Big(\dfrac{5u}{400}\Big)^2du=\dfrac{25}{160\,000}\cdot\dfrac{50^3}{3}=6.51\).
  4. Four pieces (folded + lost, on both sides): \(E=4\times6.51=26.04\).

Steps

  2. (b) \(H(f)=\dfrac{1-e^{-j2\pi fT_s}}{j2\pi f}=T_s\,\text{sinc}(\pi fT_s)\,e^{-j\pi fT_s}\); |H| is a sinc with its first zero at \(f_s\).
  3. (c) Each sample becomes a flat step of height \(g(nT_s)\) lasting \(T_s\): a staircase.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given

No signal is both time-limited and bandlimited

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • —a proof
Find

Show that a signal cannot be both time-limited and bandlimited.

The argument
  1. Suppose g is zero outside \([-T,T]\).Then \(G(f)=\int_{-T}^{T}g(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}dt\) is an analytic (smooth, entire) function of f.
  2. Suppose g is also bandlimited: \(G(f)=0\) for \(|f|>B\), i.e. G vanishes on a whole interval.
  3. An analytic function that is zero on an interval is zero everywhere.So \(G\equiv0\), hence \(g\equiv0\): contradiction.

Meaning: real (time-limited) signals are never exactly bandlimited; "bandwidth" is always an essential bandwidth, and some aliasing always exists.

Final answers
impossible (except g0)

Averaging (non-ideal) samplers: design the recovery

Spot it: averaging with q(t) = filtering g by \(Q^*(f)\) (time-reversed q), then ideal sampling (lesson 20). Recovery: LPF (B, gain \(T_s\)) then \(1/Q^*(f)\) for \(|f|\le B\). Check Q is never zero in the band.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • 5.1-12: averaging sampler with \(q_a=\Delta(\frac{t}{T_s/2})\)triangle on
  • 5.1-13: \(q_b\) = one full sine cycle on \([0,T_s]\)
Find

Design the recovery system for each.

Understand it fully

Averaging with q(t) is the same as filtering g by \(Q^*(f)\) and then sampling ideally. To recover: ideal LPF (bandwidth B, gain \(T_s\)), then undo the averaging with \(1/Q^*(f)\) over \(|f|\le B\).

5.1-12
  1. \(Q_a(f)=\dfrac{T_s}{4}\text{sinc}^2\big(\dfrac{\pi fT_s}{4}\big)\): real and never zero for \(|f|\le B
  2. Equaliser: \(E(f)=\dfrac{4}{T_s\,\text{sinc}^2(\pi fT_s/4)}\) for \(|f|\le B\).Output: g(t).
5.1-13
  1. \(Q_b(0)=0\): averaging against a full sine cycle wipes out DC and weakens all low frequencies.
  2. \(1/Q_b\) blows up at f = 0, so g can't be recovered if it has content near DC.A poor pulse choice.
Final answers
5.1-12LPF then 4/(T_s sinc²(πfT_s/4))5.1-13not recoverable near DC
Lathi 5e 5.1-14≈ 4e 6.1-3≈ 8 min

Natural sampling with rectangular pulses of width Tq at the Nyquist rate

Spot it: natural sampling → baseband term is (duty) × g. Recovery gain = 1/duty = \(T_s/T_q\) (lesson 20).

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • natural sampling with rectangular pulses of width \(T_q\) every \(T_s\), at the Nyquist rate
  • 4e: \(T_q=\frac{1}{8B}\), \(T_s=\frac{1}{2B}\); 5e (b): \(T_q=\frac1{4B}\) and \(T_q=\frac1{2B}\)
Find

The recovery filter (bandwidth, gain) and the effect of the pulse width.

Understand it fully · the duty cycle sets the gain

The pulse train with duty \(d=T_q/T_s\) is \(d+\sum\frac{2}{n\pi}\sin(n\pi d)\cos(2\pi nf_st)\). Multiplying g by it gives \(d\cdot g\) at baseband plus copies around \(nf_s\). An LPF of bandwidth B keeps \(d\cdot g\); a gain of \(1/d=T_s/T_q\) restores g.

Steps
  1. 4e / 5e (a): \(d=\dfrac{1/8B}{1/2B}=\dfrac14\) → LPF bandwidth B, gain 4.
  2. 5e (b): \(T_q=\dfrac1{4B}\) → d = ½ → gain 2.
  3. \(T_q=\dfrac1{2B}=T_s\) → d = 1: the "pulses" fill all the time, no sampling at all → gain 1.

Natural sampling never distorts g. Wider pulses send more energy (better against noise) but leave less room for other TDM channels.

Final answers
d1/4 → gain 4d1/2 → gain 2d1 → gain 1

μ-law PCM: SQNR, then trade samples for bits

Given
  • B = 1 MHz, \(f_s\) = 1.5 × Nyquist
  • L = 256, μ-law, μ = 255
  • (ii) new \(f_s\) = 1.2 × Nyquist, same bit rate
Asked

  • (ii) new SQNR in dB

Spot it: "μ-law" → \(3L^2/\ln^2(1+\mu)\) (lesson 26). "Keeping the transmission rate constant" → \(R_b=nf_s\) is fixed, so slower sampling frees bits (lesson 25).

Hint

\(R_b\) = 8 × 3 MHz. New n = \(R_b\) / new \(f_s\). Each extra bit adds 6.02 dB.

Full solution · every step, with your calculator
Given
  • \(B=1\) MHzsignal bandwidth
  • \(f_s=1.5\times\) Nyquist50% above Nyquist
  • \(L=256\) levels, μ-law with \(\mu=255\)quantiser
  • Part (ii): \(f_s=1.2\times\) Nyquist, same bit ratethe trade
Find

(i) SQNR in dB; (ii) new SQNR when sampling drops to 1.2 × Nyquist at the same bit rate.

Understand it fully · the PCM "budget"

The bit rate is the budget: \(R_b=n\times f_s\) (bits per sample × samples per second). If \(R_b\) is fixed and you take fewer samples, each sample can have more bits.

More bits → more levels (\(L=2^n\)) → smaller steps → less quantisation noise. Each extra bit doubles L; since SQNR ∝ L², that is ×4 = +6.02 dB.

For μ-law (strong compression) the SQNR is \(\dfrac{3L^2}{[\ln(1+\mu)]^2}\) (natural log!), and it doesn't depend on how loud the signal is.
